title: Aryna Sabalenka rediscovers her superpower in U.S. Open quarterfinal win over Linda Nosková
content:
NEW YORK — In a quarterfinal that offered a contrast in styles, it was the intense Aryna Sabalenka and her obvious force that overcame laid-back Linda Nosková and her stealthy power Tuesday on Arthur Ashe Stadium.

The defending U.S. Open champion knocked off this year’s Wimbledon champion 7-6(1), 3-6, 7-6(7), by reversing the narrative of her season since April.

When Nosková’s unflappability under pressure left the world No. 1 facing a 4-2 deficit in the third set — as well as the loss of her ranking — Sabalenka did not spiral to defeat, as she has done several times the past few months.

Instead, she found the indomitable poise and unstoppable power that has carried her to the top of the sport, advancing to a sixth consecutive U.S. Open semifinal.
She is sure to play an American — either the No. 3 seed Jessica Pegula or the No. 26 seed Emma Navarro — and she has the opportunity to maintain her status at the top of the game.

Sabalenka was in control early on. In the first set, Nosková worked her way back from 5-2 down to make it 5-5 then force a tiebreak, but her hard work was for naught.

She served a double fault to hand Sabalenka a 2-0 lead, which against the world No. 1, who is particularly lethal in tiebreaks, was enough to doom her. Sabalenka rolled after that, jamming Nosková on the baseline shot after shot and cruising to a 7-1 win to take the first set.

But few on tour at the moment are as good as resetting as Nosková. She did it in the Wimbledon final against Karolina Muchova; she did it in her previous two matches after losing the second set of both to rebound for a win.

She gave Sabalenka three break points in the second set that the world No. 1 failed to convert.

When it was Nosková’s turn, she didn’t waste her opportunities.

With Sabalenka serving 2-3, at 15-40, she saved one break point with a 112 mile per hour serve that Nosková couldn’t get to in time. Then, still under pressure at 30-40, Sabalenka went big on a second serve. She missed, double faulting, and Nosková had a 4-2 lead that was all she needed to sew up the second set.

Sabalenka began the third going all out, not just asserting her power but flaunting her shotmaking ability and some of the variety she’d worked so hard to add into her game at the start of the year. She stood planted in the center of the court and found short angles so sharp they caused her to sink into a squat then fall backwards when she hit them. She earned her first break point of the set early, on Nosková’s first service game at 30-40.

But Nosková shined on defense. After badly mishitting a forehand to give Sabalenka that first break point, she calmly wiped it away by redirecting a forehand far out of Sabalenka’s reach. When Sabalenka sprinted for a drop shot and hit a beautiful winner behind Nosková a point later, the 21-year-old said no problem and sent an ace straight down the middle of the T.

Two games later, Sabalenka gifted Nosková three break points after hitting a double fault down 0-30. Sabalenka saved one with a forehand cross-court winner but Nosková was lying in wait on the next serve and hammered her return to force an error out of the world No. 1. She held at love to take a 4-2 lead.

Sabalenka calmly chipped away to even things at 5-5. After holding at 6-5, she sat during the changeover with a towel over her head, blocking everything out — the noise, the pressure, the intensity of the moment. Nosková held to force a tiebreak, exactly where Sabalenka likes to be.

There, they seemed to adopt each other’s personas. Nosková was shaking her head after errors while Sabalenka thrived. She’d won nine straight tiebreaks at the U.S. Open before that deciding set. Against the Wimbledon champion, she made it an even 10, coming back from a 2-0 deficit and a wobble up 7-5 to rediscover the superpower that has eluded her for many months. When it counted at her most prolific tournament, having sent a first serve long, Sabalenka stood tall.

She paused. She hit her second serve out to Nosková’s forehand for ace. And then she roared.
